catalog_quote: Here we will base on a spoken corpus recorded in December 1999 in Bongor (Chad). We want to analyse the phonetic and phonology of tones in Masa. They have lexical and grammatical functions. But if you analyse their syntagmatic distribution in monosyllables and polysyllables, then you find that tones are somewhat conditioned by the nature of the preceding consonant or by the application of a fixed tonal pattern. We argue that Masa shows only two tonal registers and we demonstrate that by means of three rules these registers are reduced to one. Thus we could conclude that from a phonological standpoint Masa could be classified as a tonal or pitch accent language. [PDF p. 1] ... As one can see, we postulate the existence of a marked tone (H), of an unmarked tone (L or M) and of an unmarked tone + floating H (upstep). The results of the investigation allow us to conclude that Masa language …
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Masana (masa1322) is not in the catalog. The three works with stress in the title reduce to two works: Caitucoli 1980 'Tons et accent en masa goumaye' (Travaux du Cercle Linguistique de Nice 2:61-86; print-only, journal ISSN 0294-3344 not digitized per BnF; priority high, the only title naming accent in Masa) and De Dominicis 2003 'Tone or pitch accent in Masa?' (Köppe, pp. 53-72; paywalled volume PDF EUR 39.80; items 16369 and 688412 are the same chapter, the latter a CLDF duplicate with the editor as author). Not obtainable in the given list, but this search of works with stress in the title located and read the open earlier version of De Dominicis's analysis, 'The Masa tonal system' (TAPS 2001 proceedings, Bielefeld; PDF on D. Gibbon's homepage; previously recorded in our check as unreachable): Masa has three phonetic registers reduced to two phonological tones and finally to one marked H tone, hence 'a tonal or pitch accent language'; no mention of stress, H position lexically variable. Also read Melis & Platiel 1998 (Faits de langues, full text via Persée page endpoint): synchronic two-tone (marked/unmarked) analysis; the sole accent remark is a diachronic guess of an earlier initial-syllable accent (p. 464). Melis 1999 thesis abstract (theses.fr) mentions tone only. No first-hand word-stress statement for Masa was found; the language should be treated as tonal (single marked H, 'tonal accent') pending Caitucoli 1980. All files and are under Search engines, Google Books, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, BASE, HAL, Bielefeld PUB, HathiTrust, WorldCat and web.archive. finds came from Crossref, the Tuscia DSpace REST API, Gibbon's publication page, theses.fr, BnF and Glottolog.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Masa is described as a tone language with three phonetic pitch registers (H, M, L) which De Dominicis reduces to a single marked tone H: the non-high tone is realised M after non-depressor (voiceless/implosive) initials and L after depressor (voiced obstruent) initials, and three rules (consonant-conditioned register, no two adjacent marked tones with one-degree dissimilation to the right, rightward tone spreading) derive the attested word patterns; on that basis he labels Masa a 'tonal or pitch accent' language. The position of the marked H within the word is lexical (HH, HM, MH, MM, LL, LM disyllables all occur), so no fixed stress position is stated, and no source opened says anything about stress (intensity) placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose initial consonant belongs to the third set (nasals, liquids, glottal, semivowels) show genuine three-way H/M/L oppositions on the first syllable, which the two-tone / single-marked-tone analysis cannot derive (De Dominicis 2002, section 4 'Problem: the minimal pairs L/M'; Melis & Platiel 1998 pp. 458, 464-466). Trisyllables (about 5% of the vocabulary) show extra tonal variants, treated as frozen compounds (Melis & Platiel p. 461-462).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on isolated non-verbal (nominal) items and on verb aspect forms; corpus of isolated words and children's speech recorded in Bongor (Chad), December 1999, plus the lexical filing of Melis 1999 (Harra dialect, Siyeke). The 'tonal or pitch accent' label is the author's phonological reinterpretation of a 3-register (H/M/L) system as privative (one marked H tone); H is not culminative (HH, HHH patterns are attested), and nothing is said about intensity/stress placement. Melis & Platiel 1998 (the main describer) treat Masa as a tone language with 2 phonological tones and make no synchronic stress statement; their only 'accent' remark is diachronic (p. 464: an earlier stage 'devait en outre comporter un accent sur la première syllabe').
new_statements.identity_note: De Dominicis 2002 analyses a corpus recorded in Bongor, Chad (Glottolog dialect Bongor [bong1298]) together with the lexicon of Melis 1999, which describes the Harra dialect, parler de Siyeke (Chad). Melis & Platiel 1998 use Melis's Chadian data. Caitucoli 1980 (unopened) concerns 'masa goumaye' = Gumay [guma1259]. The De Dominicis Gizey papers downloaded here (2006 TAL, 2010 Studi Magrebini; 2008 SLIFO abstract) describe Gizey/Gizay [giza1238], which Glottolog 5.3 files as a dialect of Masana but De Dominicis treats as a separate language of the Masa section ('Like Masa, Gizey..'); none of them contains a stress statement.

new_statements.reading: This is a tone statement, not a word-stress statement: Masa is analysed as a language with a single marked (H) tone with lexical and grammatical (verbal aspect) functions, the other registers (M/L) being predictable from consonant-tone interference and three tonal rules; the author calls this a 'tonal or pitch accent' system. Stress is never mentioned, and the marked H has no fixed position (noun patterns with H on first, second or third syllable are listed). For catalog purposes Masa would be coded as a tone language with lexically placed H ('tonal accent'), with no fixed or weight-based stress reported by any source read; Melis & Platiel 1998 (p. 464) add only a diachronic conjecture of an earlier first-syllable accent. The unread Caitucoli 1980 'Tons et accent en masa goumaye' remains the one title that could carry an explicit synchronic accent statement.

new_statements.quote: 1.3. Tons et accent (10) Le masa possède trois tons simples : ton haut (nísí) "ils" ton moyen (kēwnā] "le couteau" ton bas (bànànà) "l'ami". [...] la mise en valeur d'une more dans l'unité accentuelle. La mise en valeur d'une more interne se réalise phonétiquement comme un ton haut. La mise en valeur de la more initiale se réalise comme l'absence de ton haut interne. [...] L'unité accentuelle est caractérisée par la présence d'un accent et d'un seul. [...] les oppositions tonales sont partiellement ou entièrement neutralisées en dehors de l'accent. [...] R. 1 : Réalisation de l'accent non initial Accent non initial - ton haut [...] les tons hauts non initiaux sont la manifestation d'un accent.
new_statements.translation: 1.3. Tones and accent. Masa has three simple tones: high (nísí 'they'), mid (kēwnā 'the knife'), low (bànànà 'the friend'). [...] the prominence given to one mora within the accentual unit. Prominence on an internal mora is realised phonetically as a high tone. Prominence on the initial mora is realised as the absence of an internal high tone. [...] The accentual unit is characterised by the presence of one accent and only one. [...] tonal oppositions are partly or entirely neutralised outside the accent. [...] Rule 1: Realisation of the non-initial accent: non-initial accent -> high tone [...] non-initial high tones are the manifestation of an accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'pitch accent' reading (De Dominicis 2002/2003) and is the earlier, more explicit source of that analysis: one culminative accent per accentual unit, realised by H tone, with tone neutralisation elsewhere. It adds the three-tone surface inventory, the mora-based definition of the accent, the enclitic domain, and the consonant-tension conditioning. No fixed placement, so it also confirms that no fixed-position stress should be recorded. Dialect: Caitucoli's data are the Goumaye variety (Moulkou), per his 1978 chapter and the title of his 1980 article.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Masa has three level tones, but Caitucoli analyses word prosody as a culminative accent: each accentual unit (word plus enclitics) carries exactly one accent on one mora; when that mora is non-initial the accent surfaces as a high tone, when it is the initial mora it surfaces as the absence of any internal high tone; tone contrasts are partly or wholly neutralised off the accent. The accent's position is not fixed (initial mora vs an internal or second mora, and in some monosyllables it moves onto the enclitic), so there is no fixed-position word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets; the definition ('un accent et d'un seul') excludes a second accent within the accentual unit.
new_statements.exceptions: Realisation depends on the tense/lax ('relâché'/'non relâché') character of the initial consonant (mid and low tone realisation, R.2-R.3); monosyllabic CV words with a non-lax initial realise their accent on the enclitic; verb forms show an 'accent interne' on the second mora when the radical ends in a vowel; the author calls the tone-accent mechanics 'très complexes' and does not present them fully in the introduction.
new_statements.identity_note: Caitucoli 1978 states that its data are the Goumaye ('masa goumaye') dialect spoken at Moulkou, canton de Toura, Chad, and his 1980 article is titled 'Tons et accent en masa goumaye'; the 1986 introduction presumably rests on the same Goumaye material. Melis 1999 describes the Harra dialect, speech of Siyeke. Matadydy 1987 is on the Massa of Bongor. De Dominicis 2003 describes 'Masa language, vùn màsànà' without a dialect label in the accessible snippet. Glottolog lists Gumay [guma1259] and Bongor among the 12 dialects of masa1322.

new_statements.quote: Dans la première partie on trouvera une analyse linguistique du Masa, dialecte Harra, parler de Siyeke [...] Dans la première qui traite de la phonologie, nous avons recensé les différentes structures syllabiques admises et avons établi l'inventaire des unîtes distinctives : consonne, voyelle, ton. L'étude du fonctionnement tonal a permis de conclure que l'opposition tonale devait être analysée en marqué s'opposant à non-marqué ; seul les termes ayant un ton non-marqué pouvant être influencés par la tendance des consonnes sonores à abaisser le registre tonal.
new_statements.translation: The first part contains a linguistic analysis of Masa, Harra dialect, the speech of Siyeke [...] In the first section, on phonology, we listed the admitted syllable structures and established the inventory of distinctive units: consonant, vowel, tone. The study of tonal functioning led to the conclusion that the tonal opposition had to be analysed as marked versus unmarked; only terms with an unmarked tone can be influenced by the tendency of voiced consonants to lower the tonal register.

readall_conflicts: No source places a fixed word stress, and none contradicts the catalog's 'pitch accent' reading. The three analyses differ in framing rather than in fact: Caitucoli 1978 presents three level tones plus contours with no accent at all; Caitucoli 1986 (and by its title 1980) reanalyses the same Goumaye data as one culminative accent per accentual unit, realised as a non-initial H tone with tonal contrasts neutralised elsewhere; Melis 1999 (abstract) and De Dominicis 2002/2003 treat the tone system as one marked tone versus unmarked, De Dominicis calling the result 'a tonal or pitch accent language'. All converge on a single marked H / accent per word whose position is lexically and morphologically determined, not fixed. The only fixed-position remark on record, Melis & Platiel 1998 p. 464 (earlier reading), is explicitly diachronic ('un système antérieur') and does not bear on the synchronic reading.

sources.citation: De Dominicis, Amedeo (2002 [workshop 2001]). The Masa tonal system. In Ulrike Gut & Dafydd Gibbon (eds), Typology of African Prosodic Systems (TAPS) Proceedings, Bielefeld University, May 18-20, 2001 (Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1), pp. 87-100. [Glottolog 53129; not in the list of works with stress in the title, found during this search of works with stress in the title; earlier check had it as 'the named source could not be reached']
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: We argue that Masa shows only two tonal registers and we demonstrate that by means of three rules these registers are reduced to one. Thus we could conclude that from a phonological standpoint Masa could be classified as a tonal or pitch accent language. [...] The results of the investigation allow us to conclude that Masa language shows only one marked tone. The other tones derive as a consequence of the application of three tonal rules and of some restrictions relative to the phonetic nature of the initial consonant of the word. Therefore Masa should be classified as a tonal or pitch accent language.
sources.locator: p. 1 (Abstract) and section 3 'The tonal system', PDF pp. 6-7 of 10 (print pp. 87-100)
sources.note: First-hand, based on a corpus recorded in Bongor, Dec. 1999. Masa is treated as a tone language: three phonetic registers H/M/L reported by earlier authors (Caitucoli 1983, Barreteau & Dieu 1986, Melis 1999) are reduced to two phonological tones (a marked H independent of the onset, an unmarked tone realized M or L by consonant-tone interference) and then to a single marked H tone, hence 'tonal or pitch accent language' (the TAPS abstract page words it 'The only phonological tone is + (tonal accent)'). The word 'stress' never occurs; no fixed position is given for the marked H: attested noun…

sources.citation: Melis, Antonio & Platiel, Suzy (1998). Le statut du ton bas en masa (Tchad). Faits de langues 11-12: 455-466. doi:10.3406/flang.1998.1227 [not in the list of works with stress in the title; found via Crossref]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: La création d'un troisième registre serait venue se surimposer à un système antérieur organisé en schèmes tonals qui devait en outre comporter un accent sur la première syllabe, comme c'est le cas pour de nombreuses langues bantoues. Ainsi cela pourrait expliquer pourquoi l'influence des consonnes sur les tons n'a porté que sur la première syllabe accentuée. [EN: The creation of a third register would have been superimposed on an earlier system organized in tonal schemes which must, moreover, have had an accent on the first syllable, as in many Bantu languages. This could explain why the consonant influence on tones affected only the first, accented syllable.]
sources.locator: p. 464, section 4 'Interprétation' (full scanned text of pp. 455-466 downloaded from Persée's per-page endpoint; the PDF itself is altcha-protected)
sources.note: Synchronically Masa (Harra dialect data of A. Melis) is described as tonal: three phonetic registers H/M/B, analysed as two phonological tones (marked H vs unmarked non-H) organized in word tonal schemes, with the initial consonant conditioning the unmarked tone on the first syllable only (pp. 457-459, 466). The only 'accent' remark is the diachronic conjecture on p. 464 that an earlier stage had an accent on the first syllable, offered to explain why consonant-tone interference is confined to the first syllable. No synchronic word-stress statement.

sources.citation: De Dominicis, Amedeo. 2002 [read at TAPS, Bielefeld, May 2001]. The Masa tonal system. In Ulrike Gut & Dafydd Gibbon (eds.), Typology of African Prosodic Systems (TAPS) Proceedings, Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1, 87-100. Bielefeld: Universität Bielefeld.

sources.note: Whole paper is on tone (corpus recorded Bongor, Dec 1999, plus Melis 1999 lexicon). Three phonetic registers H/M/L; only H is a marked tone, M/L are conditioned by the initial consonant (depressor vs non-depressor) and by three tonal rules; conclusion (PDF p. 7): 'Masa should be classified as a tonal or pitch accent language'. Nothing on stress/intensity placement; the abstract page adds 'The only phonological tone is + (tonal accent)'.
